questions.q: A positive ELISA result for HIV antibodies is usually confirmed by a more specific test called the:
questions.x: ELISA is a sensitive screening test; a positive result is confirmed by the Western blot. The Widal test is for typhoid and the Mantoux test is for tuberculosis.

questions.q: Influenza virus carries its genes as:
o: Several separate segments of single-stranded RNA
One circular molecule of double-stranded DNA
One long molecule of double-stranded RNA
questions.x: Influenza virus has a segmented genome: eight separate pieces of single-stranded RNA. Mixing of segments between strains helps produce new flu strains.

questions.q: Worldwide, the most common way in which HIV is passed from one adult to another is:
questions.x: Most adult HIV infections are acquired through unprotected sex. HIV is not spread by casual contact, droplets or insects.

questions.q: The respiratory quotient (RQ) of protein is about:
o: 0.8–0.9, between the values for fat and carbohydrate
questions.x: Proteins have an RQ of roughly 0.8–0.9, lying between fat (about 0.7) and carbohydrate (1.0). Values above 1 occur in anaerobic conditions or with oxygen-rich organic acids.

questions.q: How many rounds (cycles) of beta-oxidation are needed to break palmitic acid (16 carbons) completely into acetyl CoA?
questions.x: Sixteen carbons give eight two-carbon acetyl CoA units, but only seven cuts are needed: the last round splits a four-carbon unit into two acetyl CoA.

questions.q: Glucose is also commonly known as:
questions.x: Glucose is called grape sugar or dextrose. Fruit sugar is fructose, milk sugar is lactose and malt sugar is maltose.

questions.q: The two ends of a single RNA strand are called:
o: The amino end and the carboxyl end
The head end and the tail end
questions.x: Like DNA, an RNA strand has a 5′ end (free phosphate on carbon 5) and a 3′ end (free –OH on carbon 3). Amino and carboxyl ends belong to polypeptides.

questions.q: Glucose dissolves readily in water, but cellulose, which is made of glucose units, does not. The main reason is that in cellulose:
o: There are no –OH groups at all
The glucose units carry full electrical charges
The –OH groups are largely used in hydrogen bonds between neighbouring chains, and the molecules are very large
The chains are held together by peptide bonds
questions.x: In cellulose, long straight chains lie side by side and many –OH groups hydrogen-bond to each other. With fewer –OH groups free to bond with water, and a huge molecular size, cellulose stays insoluble.

questions.q: Some DNA sequences are transcribed into RNA that is never translated into protein. Examples of such RNA are:
questions.x: Genes for tRNA and rRNA are transcribed, and the RNA itself is the final product. Only mRNA is translated into a polypeptide.

questions.q: A polypeptide has 150 amino acids. Leaving out the stop codon, how many nucleotides in total, on both strands of the DNA, make up the stretch that codes for it?
questions.x: 150 amino acids need 150 codons, or 450 nucleotides on one strand. The DNA is double-stranded, so the stretch contains 450 × 2 = 900 nucleotides.

questions.q: By fixing the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide, a gene ultimately determines the protein's:
o: Number of copies of the gene in the cell
Rate of transcription in the nucleus
questions.x: The amino acid sequence (primary structure) decides how the chain folds, and the folded shape decides what the protein does.

questions.q: Which of the following molecules contains phosphorus?
questions.x: ATP is a nucleotide with three phosphate groups. Glucose, sucrose and cellulose are carbohydrates made only of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

questions.q: When translation begins, the first amino acid of a new polypeptide is usually:
questions.x: Translation starts at the codon AUG, which codes for methionine, so methionine is the first amino acid placed.

questions.q: In a fat molecule, the ester bonds link:
questions.x: A fat (triglyceride) forms when the –OH groups of glycerol react with the –COOH groups of fatty acids, giving ester bonds. Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds and sugars by glycosidic bonds.

questions.q: A haemoglobin molecule is made up of:
o: Four identical alpha chains with no haem group
One long chain folded into four parts
Two alpha and two beta polypeptide chains, each carrying a haem group
Two chains joined by glycosidic bonds
questions.x: Adult haemoglobin has four polypeptide chains, two alpha and two beta. Each chain holds an iron-containing haem group that binds oxygen.

questions.q: Two genes that code for two different polypeptides must differ in:
o: The type of sugar in their nucleotides
The bonds that join their nucleotides
The kinds of bases they can contain
questions.x: All genes use deoxyribose, phosphodiester bonds and the same four bases. What differs between genes is the order of the bases.

questions.q: The acrosome at the tip of a sperm head, which contains enzymes to penetrate the egg, is formed from the:
questions.x: The acrosome is a large vesicle produced by the Golgi apparatus, filled with enzymes that digest a path through the layers around the egg.

questions.q: The term 'chromosome' was first used in 1888 by:
questions.x: Waldeyer coined the word chromosome in 1888 for the threads that take up stain in a dividing nucleus. Mendel worked on inheritance, and Watson on DNA structure.

questions.q: Which type of genetic element is widely used as a vector to carry foreign genes into bacteria in genetic engineering?
questions.x: Plasmids are small circular DNA molecules that replicate on their own; a gene inserted into a plasmid can be copied in the bacterium.

questions.q: The endoplasmic reticulum was first described from electron micrographs in 1945 by:
questions.x: K. R. Porter, with Claude and Fullam, first described the ER in 1945 using the electron microscope. Singer and Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model.

questions.q: The Calvin cycle (the light-independent reactions of photosynthesis) takes place in the:
questions.x: The enzymes that fix carbon dioxide are dissolved in the stroma. The light-dependent reactions occur on the thylakoid membranes.

questions.q: A cut peripheral nerve fibre can regrow, but a cut fibre in the spinal cord usually cannot. An important reason is that peripheral fibres have a:
o: Larger number of Nissl's granules in the axon
questions.x: The neurilemma (Schwann cell sheath) of peripheral fibres guides and supports regrowth of a cut axon. Fibres in the CNS lack a neurilemma.

questions.q: The olfactory receptor cells in the nose are themselves:
o: Neurons whose own axons carry impulses towards the brain
Capsules of connective tissue around nerve endings
Muscle cells that contract when stimulated
questions.x: Olfactory receptors are modified neurons; their axons pass to the brain as the olfactory nerve. Mucus is made by other cells of the epithelium.

questions.q: A drug blocks the voltage-gated K+ channels of an axon but not its Na+ channels. The action potentials produced would show:
o: A faster return to the resting potential
questions.x: Depolarisation by Na+ still occurs, but repolarisation depends on K+ leaving through these channels, so it is slowed and the action potential lasts longer.

questions.q: A neuron receives most of its incoming signals from other neurons at its:
questions.x: Synapses from other neurons are mostly on the dendrites and cell body. Axon terminals pass signals on to the next cell.

questions.q: Which pair of functions are BOTH controlled by centres in the medulla oblongata?
o: Body temperature and rate of breathing
Rate of breathing and blood pressure
questions.x: The medulla contains the respiratory, cardiac and vasomotor centres. Balance is a cerebellum function, body temperature a hypothalamus function and vision an occipital lobe function.

questions.q: In the reflex in which the pupil narrows in bright light, impulses from the receptors travel to the brain along the:
questions.x: The receptors are in the retina, and their impulses leave the eye in the optic nerve. This is a cranial reflex, so spinal nerves are not involved.

questions.q: The corpus callosum is made up mainly of:
questions.x: The corpus callosum is a broad band of white matter: myelinated axons that cross between the two hemispheres. Neuron cell bodies make up grey matter.

questions.q: A drug blocks the acetylcholine receptors on skeletal muscle fibres. In a spinal reflex arc, which step would fail?
o: Detection of the stimulus by the receptor
Transmission from sensory neuron to interneuron
questions.x: Acetylcholine released by the motor neuron cannot act on the muscle, so the effector does not contract. The receptor, sensory neuron and synapses within the spinal cord are not affected by blocking the muscle's receptors.

questions.q: Hydrogen peroxide can be made to break down faster either by heating it or by adding catalase. The difference between the two methods is that:
o: Heating gives more molecules enough energy to cross the barrier, while catalase lowers the barrier itself
Both methods lower the activation energy
Heating lowers the activation energy, while catalase raises the energy of the molecules
Both methods raise the energy of the products
questions.x: Heat increases the kinetic energy of molecules so more exceed the activation energy. An enzyme instead reduces the activation energy needed.

questions.q: Which correctly matches a digestive enzyme with the conditions in which it works in the gut?
o: Salivary amylase – strongly alkaline small intestine
questions.x: Pepsin works best near pH 2 in the stomach. Trypsin and pancreatic lipase need the alkaline small intestine, and salivary amylase works near neutral in the mouth.

questions.q: Compared with its substrate, an enzyme molecule is usually:
o: Much smaller, so that it fits inside the substrate
About the same size, binding along its whole surface
Much larger, with only a small part forming the active site
questions.x: Enzymes are large globular proteins, while most substrates are small molecules. Only a small region, the active site, actually binds the substrate.

questions.q: An enzyme–inhibitor complex formed with a competitive inhibitor:
questions.x: While the inhibitor occupies the active site, no substrate can bind there, so no product is formed by that enzyme molecule.

questions.q: Later experiments of the Miller type, using similar gas mixtures and energy sources, also produced:
o: Sugars and the nitrogenous bases of nucleotides
Functional enzymes such as DNA polymerase
questions.x: Later workers obtained sugars, nucleotide bases such as adenine, and other monomers. No experiment has produced a living cell or a complex functional enzyme.

questions.q: RNA molecules that can act as catalysts are called:
questions.x: Ribozymes are catalytic RNA molecules. Their discovery supports the idea that early life used RNA both to store information and to speed up reactions. Ribosomes are organelles, not single molecules.

questions.q: Competition between a lion and a hyena for the same prey is an example of:
questions.x: The lion and hyena belong to different species, so their competition is interspecific. Intraspecific struggle is between members of the same species.

questions.q: The term 'chemical evolution' refers to:
o: The change in the chemistry of species after life began
The formation of organic molecules from simple inorganic substances before life existed
The breakdown of organic molecules by living cells
The evolution of new enzymes in modern bacteria
questions.x: Chemical evolution is the slow build-up of organic molecules, and then polymers, from simple inorganic gases on the early Earth, before the first cells appeared.

questions.q: The corpus luteum is kept active during the luteal phase of a cycle by:
questions.x: LH forms and supports the corpus luteum. As progesterone suppresses LH, support fades and the corpus luteum breaks down unless hCG from an embryo takes over.

questions.q: Which infection is common in people with AIDS but rare in healthy people?
questions.x: Pneumocystis pneumonia is a typical opportunistic infection in AIDS; it rarely causes illness when the immune system is normal. Tuberculosis is also common in AIDS.

questions.q: A pregnant woman has active genital herpes sores at the time of delivery. The main risk is that:
o: The baby will be born with syphilis
The baby may be infected during birth and become seriously ill
The baby will be born with sickle-cell anaemia
The mother will become sterile immediately
questions.x: Herpes can pass to the baby during passage through the birth canal, and newborn herpes can be severe. Doctors may advise a caesarean delivery in such cases.

questions.q: A cross-section through the overlap region of the A band shows each thick filament surrounded by:
o: Two thin filaments, one on each side
Six thin filaments in a hexagonal pattern
Twelve thick filaments in a ring
questions.x: Where thick and thin filaments overlap, each thick filament is surrounded by six thin filaments arranged in a hexagon. This allows its myosin heads to reach thin filaments on all sides.

questions.q: Why do crystals form in the joints in gout?
o: Calcium is drawn out of the bones into the joint fluid
Uric acid is poorly soluble, so at high levels it comes out of solution
Synovial fluid freezes in cold joints
questions.x: Uric acid dissolves poorly in body fluids; when its level rises too high it crystallises as needle-shaped urate crystals in joints. The crystals are not calcium or cartilage fragments.

questions.q: The swelling of a joint affected by arthritis is partly due to:
o: The bones of the joint growing longer
Loss of all the synovial fluid
Extra fluid collecting in the joint cavity
questions.x: Inflammation makes the synovial membrane produce extra fluid, which collects in the joint and makes it swell. Bones do not lengthen, and losing fluid would not cause swelling.

questions.q: The nuclei of skeletal muscle fibres lie at the edge of the fibre. In a cardiac muscle cell, the nucleus lies:
o: At both ends of the cell
Near the centre of the cell
questions.x: Cardiac muscle cells have one (sometimes two) centrally placed nuclei, unlike the many peripheral nuclei of skeletal fibres.

questions.q: One cross-bridge cycle moves a thin filament only a very short distance. A sarcomere can still shorten a lot because:
o: Each power stroke breaks the thin filament into pieces
The thick filaments shorten after each stroke
Each myosin head attaches, pulls and detaches many times
The Z lines move apart between strokes
questions.x: Many myosin heads cycle repeatedly, each time attaching further along the actin, like hands pulling a rope. The filaments do not shorten or break, and the Z lines move closer together, not apart.

questions.q: Growth in the length of a long bone stops when:
o: Red marrow appears in the shaft
The epiphyseal (growth) plates are replaced by bone
questions.x: A long bone lengthens at its cartilage growth plates. At the end of puberty these plates ossify and fuse the ends to the shaft, so growth in length stops.

questions.q: Which property of the sarcolemma lets a skeletal muscle fibre respond to its motor neuron?
o: It is excitable and can conduct an action potential
It is fully permeable to every ion
It contains the contractile proteins actin and myosin
It stores calcium ions inside its folds
questions.x: Like a neuron's membrane, the sarcolemma is excitable: it can depolarise and carry an action potential over the fibre and into the T-tubules. Calcium is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, not in the sarcolemma.

questions.q: Spongy bone differs from compact bone in that spongy bone:
o: Has no mineral salts in its matrix
Is found only in the shaft of long bones
questions.x: Spongy bone is a network of thin bony bars without osteons. It still has osteocytes and mineralised matrix, and it lies mainly in the ends of long bones, not the shaft.

questions.q: A dihybrid cross RrYy × RrYy yields 640 seeds. The expected number of rryy seeds is:
questions.x: P(rryy) = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16, and 640 ÷ 16 = 40. 120 would be each 3/16 class and 360 the 9/16 class.

questions.q: From the results of a test cross, how can you tell whether a linked dihybrid had its genes in coupling or in repulsion?
o: From which two offspring classes are the most frequent
From the total number of offspring
From whether all four classes appear
From the phenotype of the recessive tester
questions.x: The most frequent classes are the parental types, showing the allele combinations on the parent's chromosomes. AaBb and aabb most common means coupling; Aabb and aaBb means repulsion.

questions.q: The hemophilia allele of an affected man most often shows up again in his:
questions.x: He passes Xʰ to all his daughters, who are carriers, and they pass it to about half their sons. His sons get his Y, not the allele.

questions.q: A and B are completely dominant and unlinked. Which cross gives offspring in a 1 : 1 phenotypic ratio?
o: Heterozygous for one gene, homozygous dominant for the other × double recessive
questions.x: AaBB × aabb gives AaBb and aaBb in equal numbers: all show B and half show A, so 1 : 1. AaBb × aabb gives 1 : 1 : 1 : 1, AABB × aabb gives one class, and AaBb × AaBb gives 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

questions.q: In the cross AaBb × AaBb, what fraction of the offspring shows the recessive phenotype for gene A but the dominant phenotype for gene B?
questions.x: P(aa) = 1/4 and P(B_) = 3/4, so P(aaB_) = 1/4 × 3/4 = 3/16. This is one of the two 3/16 classes of the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.

questions.q: In male Drosophila, crossing over normally does not occur. As a result, linked genes in males show:
questions.x: Without crossing over, linked genes are never separated, which is complete linkage. Incomplete linkage needs occasional crossing over, as in female Drosophila.

questions.q: Genes located on the same chromosome are said to be:
questions.x: Genes on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together. Alleles are forms of one gene at one locus, and genes on different chromosomes assort independently.

questions.q: Which person can NOT pass the hemophilia allele to any of his or her children?
o: A woman whose father had hemophilia
questions.x: A man with normal clotting is XᴴY and has no Xʰ to pass on. A woman with normal clotting could still be a carrier.

questions.q: How many valves guard the openings of the chambers of the human heart?
o: Two: one on each side of the heart
Four: two atrioventricular and two semilunar
Six: one for each great vessel
questions.x: There are four heart valves: tricuspid and bicuspid (atrioventricular), and the aortic and pulmonary semilunar valves.

questions.q: Before lymph is returned to the blood, it normally passes through:
o: One or more lymph nodes, where it is filtered
The kidneys, where it is cleaned
The heart, where it is pumped
The liver, where it is detoxified
questions.x: Lymph vessels pass through lymph nodes, which filter out pathogens and debris before the lymph reaches the ducts and veins.

questions.q: While the ventricles are in systole, the atria are:
o: Contracting and pushing blood into the ventricles
Contracting and pushing blood into the veins
Relaxed and filling with blood from the veins
questions.x: Atria and ventricles never contract at the same moment. During ventricular systole the atria are in diastole and refill from the venae cavae and pulmonary veins.

questions.q: Varicose veins, which are swollen and twisted, usually develop when:
o: Fat is deposited inside the arteries
Lymph vessels are blocked by worms
Valves in the veins become weak, so blood collects in the veins
questions.x: When venous valves fail, blood flows back and pools, stretching the vein walls, often in the legs. Fatty deposits in arteries cause atherosclerosis instead.

questions.q: The normal heart sounds heard with a stethoscope are produced mainly by the:
o: Flow of blood in the coronary arteries
questions.x: 'Lubb' and 'dubb' are made by the valves snapping shut: first the atrioventricular valves, then the semilunar valves. Muscle contraction and nerve impulses are silent.

questions.q: An antibody binds to its antigen because:
o: Both are made of the same nucleic acid
Their shapes are complementary, fitting like a lock and key
The antibody digests the antigen with enzymes
Any antibody can attach to any antigen
questions.x: The antigen-binding site has a shape complementary to one antigenic determinant, so binding is specific, like a key in a lock. Antibodies do not digest antigens.

questions.q: A vaccine protects a person by:
o: Stimulating the body to make its own antibodies and memory cells
Supplying ready-made antibodies from a horse
Killing all bacteria in the body at once
questions.x: A vaccine contains antigens that trigger the person's own immune response, leaving memory cells that give long-lasting protection. Ready-made antibodies give only passive immunity.

questions.q: Blood that has been oxygenated in the lungs returns to the heart through the:
o: Pulmonary arteries, into the right atrium
Pulmonary veins, into the left atrium
Venae cavae, into the right atrium
questions.x: The pulmonary veins are the only veins that carry oxygen-rich blood; they empty into the left atrium. The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

questions.q: The layer of the pleura that is attached directly to the surface of the lung is the:
questions.x: The visceral pleura covers the lung itself, while the parietal pleura lines the inside of the thoracic wall and diaphragm. The pericardium surrounds the heart and the peritoneum lines the abdomen.

questions.q: In the neck, the larynx (voice box) lies between the:
questions.x: Air passes from the pharynx into the larynx and then down into the trachea. The larynx sits at the top of the trachea and contains the vocal cords.

questions.q: Food entering the stomach from the oesophagus passes through which regions of the stomach, in order, before reaching the duodenum?
questions.x: Food enters at the cardiac end (near the heart), is churned in the large body, with the fundus bulging above, and leaves through the pyloric region and pyloric sphincter into the duodenum.

questions.q: The mucus that protects and lubricates the lining of the intestine is secreted by scattered cells in its epithelium called:
questions.x: Goblet cells are mucus-secreting cells scattered among the columnar cells of the intestinal lining. Parietal and chief cells are in gastric glands, and Kupffer cells are in the liver.

questions.q: Pepsin works best in a medium that is:
questions.x: Pepsin works in the stomach, where hydrochloric acid keeps the pH at about 2. Pancreatic enzymes, by contrast, work in the slightly alkaline duodenum.

questions.q: Blood flows slowly through the long vasa recta. This is useful because:
o: It does not wash away the high solute concentration of the medulla
It allows plasma proteins to be filtered
It raises the blood pressure in the cortex
questions.x: A fast flow would carry away the salt and urea that make the medulla hypertonic. Slow flow in the hairpin vasa recta preserves this gradient, so concentrated urine can still be made.

questions.q: During urination (micturition), which events take place?
o: The bladder wall relaxes and the urethral sphincters contract
The ureters contract and the bladder wall relaxes
The kidneys contract and push urine into the bladder
The smooth muscle of the bladder wall contracts and the urethral sphincters relax
questions.x: To empty the bladder its muscular wall contracts while the sphincters around the urethra open. When sphincters contract and the wall relaxes, urine is stored instead.

questions.q: The desert fox has very large ears while the Arctic fox has small ears. Large ears suit the desert fox because they:
o: Give a large surface area for losing heat
Trap air to insulate the head
Reduce blood flow to the skin
questions.x: Thin ears with many blood vessels act as radiators. In the cold, small ears reduce heat loss.

questions.q: Which of these is a treatment for kidney stones rather than a cause of them?
o: High uric acid in the blood
questions.x: Lithotripsy breaks stones into pieces. Dehydration, high oxalate intake and high uric acid all raise the risk of stones.

questions.q: Bowman's capsule is best described as:
o: The cup-shaped, double-walled blind end of a nephron around the glomerulus
A tuft of capillaries lying between two arterioles
The fibrous covering of the whole kidney
The funnel at the upper end of the ureter
questions.x: Bowman's capsule is the expanded, cup-like start of the nephron. Its two walls enclose a space that receives the filtrate; the capillary tuft inside it is the glomerulus.

questions.q: ADH travels from the posterior pituitary to its target cells in the kidney through the:
questions.x: ADH is a hormone, so it is released into the blood and carried to the DCT and collecting duct cells. Nerves carry impulses, not hormones, to the kidney.

questions.q: An elderly man with a greatly enlarged prostate gland develops kidney failure. The likely reason is that the prostate:
o: Blocks urine outflow, so pressure builds back up into the kidneys
Destroys red blood cells in the kidney
Stops the glomeruli from receiving blood
questions.x: The prostate surrounds the urethra. If it obstructs urine flow, urine backs up and the rising pressure damages the kidneys.

questions.q: Mammalian embryos can safely excrete soluble urea, unlike embryos in shelled eggs, because:
o: Urea passes across the placenta into the mother's blood and is removed by her kidneys
Mammalian embryos produce no nitrogenous waste
Urea is insoluble and stays in the uterus
The embryo's liver converts urea into uric acid
questions.x: Inside a sealed egg, waste must be stored, so insoluble uric acid is needed. A mammal's embryo hands its urea to the mother through the placenta.

questions.q: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus trigger more ADH release when they detect:
o: A fall in the solute concentration of the blood
A rise in blood glucose only
A rise in the solute concentration of the blood
questions.x: When blood becomes too concentrated, as when water is short, the osmoreceptors stimulate ADH release so that more water is kept. A diluted blood switches ADH release down.

questions.q: In the first gene therapy for ADA-deficient SCID, treatment had to be repeated every few months because:
o: The patient's body destroyed the ADA enzyme in the blood
The gene was inserted into the patient's red blood cells
The bacteria used as vectors kept dying
The corrected white blood cells had a limited lifespan and were not stem cells
questions.x: The normal ADA gene was put into the patient's T lymphocytes, which die after some time. As they were not stem cells, new corrected cells were not produced, so fresh treated cells had to be given again.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT added to a PCR reaction mixture?
questions.x: PCR needs template DNA, two primers, the four nucleotides and a heat-stable polymerase in buffer. Ligase joins DNA fragments in gene cloning and is not used to copy DNA in PCR.

questions.q: Monoclonal antibodies made entirely from mouse cells often stop working when given repeatedly to a patient because:
o: Mouse antibodies are too small to bind antigens
They are digested by the patient's red blood cells
The patient's immune system makes antibodies against the foreign mouse protein
They change into hormones in the human body
questions.x: Mouse proteins are foreign to humans, so repeated doses trigger an immune response that destroys them. Scientists therefore make 'humanised' antibodies that are mostly human in structure.

questions.q: For 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, 4.6 g of sodium reacts with excess chlorine. If the percentage yield is 50%, what mass of NaCl is obtained? (Na = 23, Cl = 35.5)
questions.x: Na = 4.6/23 = 0.2 mol gives 0.2 mol NaCl = 0.2 × 58.5 = 11.7 g in theory; 50% of this is 5.85 g. 11.7 g is the theoretical yield.

questions.q: For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 6 g of H₂ is exploded with 32 g of O₂. When the reaction is complete, the vessel contains: (H = 1, O = 16)
o: 38 g of water and nothing else
36 g of water and 2 g of hydrogen
54 g of water and no oxygen
36 g of water and 16 g of oxygen
questions.x: H₂ = 3 mol, O₂ = 1 mol; O₂ is limiting and makes 2 mol (36 g) of water using 2 mol H₂, so 1 mol (2 g) of H₂ remains. Total mass stays 38 g, as it must.

questions.q: When a copper atom (Z = 29) loses one electron, the configuration of the ion formed is:
questions.x: Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, and the 4s electron is lost first, so Cu⁺ is [Ar] 3d¹⁰.

questions.q: A light paddle wheel placed in the path of positive rays begins to rotate. This shows that positive rays:
o: Are a form of electromagnetic radiation
Consist of material particles that possess momentum
questions.x: Turning the paddle wheel shows that the rays are made of particles with mass and velocity, i.e. momentum. Their deflection by fields shows separately that they are charged.

questions.q: What is the frequency of radiation whose photons each carry 6.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J? (Planck's constant = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
questions.x: ν = E/h = 6.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ = 1 × 10¹⁵ Hz. Multiplying E by h instead of dividing gives the meaningless 4.4 × 10⁻⁵².

questions.q: For 1 mol of an ideal gas at 273 K, the product PV is about: (R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
questions.x: PV = nRT = 1 × 0.0821 × 273 ≈ 22.4 dm³ atm. This is why 1 mol occupies 22.4 dm³ at 1 atm and 273 K.

questions.q: A gas is heated from 27 °C to 327 °C. The average kinetic energy of its molecules:
questions.x: Average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature: 27 °C = 300 K and 327 °C = 600 K, so it doubles. The 12-fold answer comes from wrongly using Celsius temperatures.

questions.q: A balloon holds 2.00 dm³ of air at 0 °C. It is warmed to 100 °C at constant pressure. Its new volume is about:
questions.x: V₂ = V₁ × T₂/T₁ = 2.00 × 373/273 ≈ 2.73 dm³. The 1.46 dm³ value comes from inverting the temperature ratio.

questions.q: Volumes of gases are usually compared at STP because:
o: All gases have the same mass at STP
Gases do not expand or contract at STP
The volume of a gas depends on its temperature and pressure, so fixed reference conditions are needed
Gases behave as liquids at STP
questions.x: A gas volume changes with both temperature and pressure, so it is only meaningful to compare volumes under agreed standard conditions. Gases still expand and contract at STP.

questions.q: Water needs a large amount of heat to change into vapour (a high enthalpy of vaporisation) mainly because:
o: Covalent O–H bonds must be broken
Many hydrogen bonds between molecules must be broken
Water has only weak London forces
questions.x: Vaporisation separates molecules, so the extensive hydrogen bonding between water molecules must be overcome. The O–H bonds inside each molecule stay intact.

questions.q: In which molecular crystal are the molecules held together mainly by hydrogen bonds?
questions.x: Water molecules in ice are linked by O–H···O hydrogen bonds. Iodine, dry ice and solid argon are held only by weak London forces.

questions.q: In a cubic unit cell, atoms of element M occupy all 8 corners and an atom of element Z occupies the body centre. The simplest formula of the compound is:
questions.x: Corners give 8 × 1/8 = 1 atom of M, and the body centre gives 1 atom of Z, so the ratio is 1 : 1. M₈Z forgets that corner atoms are shared.

questions.q: For which reaction is Kp equal to Kc?
questions.x: Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, so they are equal when Δn = 0. For N₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2NO there are 2 mol of gas on each side.

questions.q: Which of these reactions is reversible under ordinary conditions in a closed vessel?
o: Precipitation of AgCl from AgNO₃ and NaCl solutions
questions.x: N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ readily goes both ways and sets up an equilibrium. The other three go practically to completion.

questions.q: In a chemical equation, the sign ⇌ shows that the reaction is:
questions.x: The double half-arrow shows that the reaction can go both ways: reactants form products and products re-form reactants.

questions.q: On a Maxwell–Boltzmann energy distribution curve, the area under the curve to the right of the activation energy represents:
o: The fraction of molecules with enough energy to react
The total number of molecules in the sample
The enthalpy change of the reaction
The fraction of molecules that are products
questions.x: Only molecules with energy equal to or greater than Ea can react on collision; their number is the area beyond Ea.

questions.q: On an energy profile, the activation energy of the forward reaction is the energy difference between:
o: The activated complex and the reactants
The activated complex and the products
questions.x: Ea (forward) is the height of the barrier measured from the reactants to the peak. The reactant–product gap is ΔH.

questions.q: Anhydrous CuSO₄ dissolves in water with ΔH = −66 kJ mol⁻¹, and CuSO₄·5H₂O dissolves with ΔH = +12 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(l) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s)?
questions.x: Both salts give the same solution, so ΔH(hydration) = −66 − (+12) = −78 kJ mol⁻¹. This ΔH cannot be measured directly, so Hess's law is used.

questions.q: For a reaction at constant pressure, ΔH = ΔE + PΔV. ΔH is greater than ΔE when:
o: The volume of the system decreases
No gases take part in the reaction
The reaction is carried out at constant volume
Gas is produced, so the volume of the system increases
questions.x: If the volume increases, PΔV is positive, so ΔH = ΔE + PΔV is larger than ΔE, e.g. CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. With no change in volume the two are equal.

questions.q: A sealed glass flask containing a gas is heated from outside. The gas in the flask is an example of:
questions.x: A closed system can exchange energy, here heat through the glass, but not matter, because the flask is sealed.

questions.q: E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V and E°(I₂/I⁻) = +0.54 V. When Fe³⁺ and I⁻ ions are mixed in solution under standard conditions:
o: I₂ is formed by reduction of I⁻
No reaction occurs between Fe³⁺ and I⁻
questions.x: Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ has the higher E°, so Fe³⁺ is reduced and I⁻ is oxidised: 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂ (E°cell = +0.23 V).

questions.q: Burning magnesium continues to burn in carbon dioxide: 2Mg + CO₂ → 2MgO + C. In this reaction CO₂ acts as:
o: A reducing agent, as carbon is oxidised from 0 to +4
A reducing agent, as oxygen is oxidised
An oxidising agent, as carbon is reduced from +4 to 0
Neither, since no electrons are transferred
questions.x: Magnesium is oxidised (0 to +2) and carbon in CO₂ is reduced (+4 to 0), so CO₂ is the oxidising agent.

questions.q: The hybridisation of the carbon atom in carbon dioxide, O=C=O, is:
questions.x: Carbon forms two σ bonds and has no lone pair, so it uses two sp hybrid orbitals at 180°. Its two remaining p orbitals form the two π bonds.

questions.q: In tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, carbon has four bond pairs and no lone pair. The shape of CCl₄ is:
questions.x: Four bond pairs with no lone pair get as far apart as possible in a tetrahedral arrangement, with angles of 109.5°.

questions.q: When VSEPR theory is applied to CO₂, each C=O double bond is treated as:
o: Two separate bond pairs pointing in different directions
One bonding region, like a single bond
A lone pair on the carbon atom
questions.x: For predicting shape, a double or triple bond counts as one region of electron density. Carbon in CO₂ therefore has two regions, which lie at 180°.

questions.q: Magnesium reacts with cold water at first, but the reaction soon almost stops. The main reason is that:
o: Magnesium becomes coated with magnesium chloride
A layer of sparingly soluble Mg(OH)₂ forms on the surface
Hydrogen gas dissolves in the water
questions.x: Mg + 2H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ + H₂; the hydroxide is almost insoluble and coats the metal, slowing further attack. Hot water or steam reacts faster.

questions.q: A first-row transition metal ion has a spin-only magnetic moment of 3.87 BM. Using μ = √(n(n + 2)), the number of unpaired electrons, n, is:
questions.x: n = 3 gives √(3 × 5) = √15 ≈ 3.87 BM. n = 2 gives √8 ≈ 2.83 BM and n = 4 gives √24 ≈ 4.90 BM.

questions.q: Butane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃, is classified as:
questions.x: Its four carbon atoms are joined one after another with no ring and no branch. Its isomer 2-methylpropane is the branched-chain form.

questions.q: The rotation of plane-polarised light by an optically active compound is measured with a:
questions.x: A polarimeter measures the angle and direction through which a solution rotates plane-polarised light.

questions.q: 1,2-dibromoethane is warmed with zinc dust (instead of being heated with alcoholic KOH). The organic product is:
questions.x: Zinc removes the two bromine atoms from adjacent carbons (dehalogenation), forming only one π bond, so ethene is formed. Ethyne by this method needs a tetrahalide.

questions.q: The addition of chlorine to benzene in bright sunlight takes place by:
questions.x: Sunlight splits Cl₂ into chlorine free radicals, which add to the ring. With FeCl₃ in the dark the reaction would instead be electrophilic substitution.

questions.q: Rank hex-1-ene, benzene and hexane by how readily each is attacked by electrophiles.
questions.x: The localised π electrons of hex-1-ene are most available. Benzene's delocalised π electrons react only with strong electrophiles and a catalyst. Hexane has no π electrons and does not react with electrophiles.

questions.q: 1,2-dibromobutane, CH₂BrCHBrCH₂CH₃, is heated with alcoholic KOH and then treated with sodamide (NaNH₂). The main organic product is:
questions.x: Two molecules of HBr are eliminated from the neighbouring carbons C1 and C2, so the triple bond forms between them, giving CH≡CCH₂CH₃.

questions.q: Which equation shows how the electrophile is produced in the chlorination of benzene with FeCl₃?
questions.x: The Lewis acid FeCl₃ accepts a chloride ion from Cl₂, leaving the chloronium electrophile Cl⁺. Splitting Cl₂ into radicals happens only in light.

questions.q: During further chlorination of chloromethane, a chlorine radical removes a hydrogen atom from CH₃Cl. The radical formed is:
questions.x: Cl• + CH₃Cl → •CH₂Cl + HCl. This radical then reacts with Cl₂ to give CH₂Cl₂ and a new Cl•.

questions.q: Silver acetylide is warmed with dilute nitric acid. What happens?
o: Silver acetylide dissolves to give ethanal
questions.x: The acid supplies H⁺ to the acetylide ion, giving back ethyne: Ag₂C₂ + 2HNO₃ → C₂H₂ + 2AgNO₃. This can be used to recover pure ethyne.

questions.q: Butyl iodide, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂I, has the IUPAC name:
questions.x: The four-carbon chain is numbered from the end nearer the iodine, giving 1-iodobutane. Numbering from the other end (4-iodo) does not give the lowest locant.

questions.q: Ethanol is warmed with sodium bromide and concentrated sulphuric acid, which together produce HBr. The organic product is:
questions.x: HBr substitutes Br for the –OH group: C₂H₅OH + HBr → C₂H₅Br + H₂O. 1,2-Dibromoethane would need Br₂ adding across ethene.

questions.q: Which of the following is a primary alcohol?
questions.x: In (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH (2-methylpropan-1-ol) the –OH carbon is joined to only one other carbon, so it is primary. (CH₃)₂CHOH and butan-2-ol are secondary; (CH₃)₃COH is tertiary.

questions.q: For electrophilic substitution on the benzene ring, the –OH group of phenol is classified as:
questions.x: The –OH group donates electron density to the ring, increasing the rate (activating), and the extra density builds up at the ortho and para positions, so it directs there.

questions.q: In the silver mirror test, how many moles of Ag⁺ are reduced to silver for each mole of propanal oxidised?
questions.x: The aldehyde is oxidised to a carboxylate, losing two electrons per molecule; each Ag⁺ gains one electron, so 2 mol Ag⁺ are reduced: RCHO + 2Ag⁺ → ... + 2Ag.

questions.q: Ethanal is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate. The organic product is:
questions.x: Aldehydes are easily oxidised: CH₃CHO + [O] → CH₃COOH. Ethanol would be the reduction product.

questions.q: The general formula of saturated monocarboxylic acids is:
questions.x: An alkyl group CₙH₂ₙ₊₁ joined to –COOH gives the series HCOOH (n = 0), CH₃COOH, C₂H₅COOH and so on. –CHO belongs to aldehydes.

questions.q: Pepsin, a protein-digesting enzyme of the stomach, works best at a pH of about:
questions.x: Each enzyme has an optimum pH. Pepsin works in the strongly acidic stomach, so its optimum is about pH 2; at pH 7 or above its activity is very low.

questions.q: Alizarin, a red mordant dye, was originally obtained from:
o: The roots of the madder plant
The leaves of the indigo plant
questions.x: Alizarin was extracted from madder roots before it was made synthetically. Indigo leaves give the blue dye indigo, and cochineal insects give a crimson dye.

questions.q: A vector of magnitude 10 N points 30° below the positive x-axis. Its x- and y-components are (cos 30° = √3/2, sin 30° = 0.5):
questions.x: x = 10 cos 30° = 5√3 N, and y = −10 sin 30° = −5 N because the vector points below the x-axis. Swapping sin and cos gives the wrong pair.

questions.q: Two ice skaters at rest on smooth ice push each other apart. Which quantities are equal in magnitude for the two skaters?
o: Their speeds and their kinetic energies
The forces on them and their changes in momentum
questions.x: By the third law the forces are equal and opposite and act for the same time, so the momentum changes are equal. Unequal masses give unequal accelerations, speeds and kinetic energies.

questions.q: The SI unit of linear momentum is:
questions.x: Momentum = mass × velocity, so its unit is kg × m s⁻¹ = kg m s⁻¹ (equivalent to N s). kg m s⁻² is the newton, the unit of force.

questions.q: A 10 g bullet moving at 300 m s⁻¹ embeds itself in a 2.99 kg wooden block resting on a smooth surface. The block and bullet move off at:
questions.x: Momentum before = 0.01 × 300 = 3 kg m s⁻¹. Total mass after = 3 kg, so v = 3 ÷ 3 = 1 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: At t = 0, car P is at x = 0 moving at a constant 10 m s⁻¹, and car Q is at x = 60 m moving at a constant 5 m s⁻¹ in the same direction. Their displacement–time lines meet at t =
questions.x: P's position is 10t and Q's is 60 + 5t. They meet when 10t = 60 + 5t, so t = 12 s. 6 s wrongly uses P's speed alone (60 ÷ 10).

questions.q: The acceleration of a train increases steadily from zero as time passes. Its velocity–time graph is:
o: A curve that becomes steeper with time
A curve that becomes flatter with time
questions.x: The slope of a velocity–time graph is acceleration. If acceleration keeps increasing, the slope keeps increasing, so the graph curves upward more and more steeply.

questions.q: A light ball moving at 8 m s⁻¹ strikes a heavier ball at rest head-on, perfectly elastically, and bounces straight back at 2 m s⁻¹. The speed of the heavier ball after the collision is:
questions.x: Relative speed of separation = approach = 8 m s⁻¹. Taking forward as positive: v − (−2) = 8, so v = 6 m s⁻¹. 10 m s⁻¹ wrongly treats the rebound as forward.

questions.q: A 60 kg person climbs a staircase and gains 18 kJ of gravitational potential energy. The height climbed is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
questions.x: h = PE ÷ mg = 18 000 ÷ 600 = 30 m. Forgetting the 'kilo' in 18 kJ gives 0.03 m, and dividing by m only gives 300 m.

questions.q: A 100 W bulb is left on for 10 hours. The electrical energy it uses is:
questions.x: Energy = power × time = 0.1 kW × 10 h = 1 kWh. Using 100 instead of 0.1 kW gives the 1000 kWh error.

questions.q: Body X has the same linear momentum as body Y, but X has only half the mass of Y. KE of X : KE of Y is:
questions.x: With equal momentum, KE = p²/2m is inversely proportional to mass, so X, with half the mass, has twice the kinetic energy of Y.

questions.q: A satellite completes one orbit every 90 minutes. Taking π = 3.14, its angular velocity is about:
questions.x: T = 90 × 60 = 5400 s, ω = 2π/T = 6.28/5400 ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻³ rad s⁻¹. Using minutes instead of seconds gives 7.0 × 10⁻².

questions.q: Wind blows at 20 m s⁻¹ across a flat roof while the air inside the house is still. Taking the density of air as 1.2 kg m⁻³, the pressure difference across the roof is:
questions.x: ΔP = ½ρv² = 0.5 × 1.2 × 400 = 240 Pa, with the higher pressure inside. Leaving out the ½ gives 480 Pa; forgetting to square v gives 12 Pa.

questions.q: The normal diastolic blood pressure of a healthy adult is about:
questions.x: Normal blood pressure is about 120/80 mmHg (torr): 120 is the systolic and 80 the diastolic pressure.

questions.q: In Bernoulli's equation, the pressure P of the fluid can be interpreted as:
o: Pressure energy (work done by pressure) per unit volume
questions.x: The work done by pressure in pushing a volume V into the tube is PV, so P is the work (pressure energy) per unit volume. That is why it can be added to ½ρv².

questions.q: Which change would INCREASE the air drag on a car moving along a road?
o: Giving the car a more streamlined shape
Lowering the car's roof rack and luggage
questions.x: Fluid drag increases with the speed of the body relative to the fluid. Streamlining, a smaller frontal area and removing roof luggage all reduce drag.

questions.q: In a longitudinal wave, compressions correspond to which feature of a transverse wave?
questions.x: Compressions are regions of maximum crowding, matching the crests of a transverse wave; rarefactions match the troughs. A wavelength is the distance between two consecutive compressions.

questions.q: Two people talk at the same time in a room, and a listener can still pick out each voice. This is possible because:
o: Sound waves from one person absorb those of the other
Only one sound wave can exist in the air at a time
Sound waves from different people cancel completely
Sound waves pass through each other and continue unchanged
questions.x: When waves overlap their displacements simply add, and after crossing each wave carries on with its own form. So each voice reaches the listener unaltered.

questions.q: Two nodes of a stationary wave are 2λ apart. How many antinodes lie between them?
questions.x: Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart, so a distance of 2λ holds 4 loops, each with one antinode at its centre.

questions.q: Two loudspeakers driven in phase by one generator produce sound of wavelength 2 m. Which of the following path differences gives a loud sound?
questions.x: Loud (constructive) points have path difference nλ: 0, 2, 4, 6 m. 1, 3 and 5 m are odd multiples of λ/2 = 1 m, which give quiet points.

questions.q: Two loudspeakers driven in phase emit sound of frequency 510 Hz; the speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. At a point where the path difference is 1.0 m, there is:
o: Constructive interference, since the path difference is 1.5λ
Constructive interference, since the path difference is λ
Destructive interference, since the path difference is λ/2
Destructive interference, since the path difference is 1.5λ
questions.x: λ = 340/510 = 2/3 m, so 1.0 m = 1.5λ, an odd multiple of λ/2. The interference there is destructive.

questions.q: A pipe open at both ends can produce:
o: All harmonics, both odd and even
questions.x: With an antinode at each open end, any whole number of half-wavelengths fits, so an open pipe gives all harmonics. A pipe closed at one end gives only odd ones.

questions.q: When a gas expands and pushes back its surroundings, the work done by the gas is:
questions.x: In an expansion the gas pushes the piston outward in the direction of its force, so the work done by the gas is positive.

questions.q: Two bodies at exactly the same temperature but with different masses are placed in contact. The net flow of heat between them is:
o: From the larger body to the smaller one
From the smaller body to the larger one
From the body with more internal energy to the other
questions.x: Net heat flow depends only on a temperature difference. With equal temperatures there is none, whatever the masses or internal energies.

questions.q: A proton and an electron are placed, one at a time, at the same point in an electric field. The electric forces on them are:
o: Equal in magnitude and in the same direction
Equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
Larger on the proton, because its mass is larger
Larger on the electron, because its mass is smaller
questions.x: F = qE depends on charge, not mass. Proton and electron have equal and opposite charges, so the forces are equal in size and opposite in direction (their accelerations differ, not the forces).

questions.q: The equipotential surfaces around an isolated point charge are:
o: Concentric spheres centred on the charge
Straight lines radiating from the charge
Cylinders around a line through the charge
questions.x: V = kq/r is the same at all points at the same distance r, so each equipotential is a sphere centred on the charge. The radial lines are the field lines, perpendicular to these spheres.

questions.q: A charge of −3 μC placed at a point experiences a force of 6 × 10⁻³ N directed due north. The electric field at that point is:
questions.x: E = F/|q| = 6 × 10⁻³ / 3 × 10⁻⁶ = 2000 N C⁻¹. The force on a negative charge is opposite to the field, so the field points due south.

questions.q: A source of emf 6 V and internal resistance 2 Ω is first connected to a 1 Ω load and then to a 2 Ω load. The power in the load:
questions.x: With 1 Ω: I = 6 ÷ 3 = 2 A, P = 2² × 1 = 4 W. With 2 Ω: I = 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 A, P = 1.5² × 2 = 4.5 W, the maximum, since R now equals r.

questions.q: A cell of emf 2 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is connected to a 3.5 Ω resistor. The current in the circuit is:
questions.x: I = E ÷ (R + r) = 2 ÷ (3.5 + 0.5) = 0.5 A. Ignoring r gives 0.57 A.

questions.q: What force acts on an alpha particle (charge 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) travelling at 5 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.2 T field?
questions.x: F = qvB = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 5 × 10⁵ × 0.2 = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ N. Using the charge of a single proton gives half this value.

questions.q: For a straight conductor of length L carrying current I at right angles to a uniform field, the magnetic flux density is defined by:
questions.x: From F = ILB sin 90° = ILB, the flux density is B = F/(IL), the force per unit current per unit length.

questions.q: A grid line's voltage is raised from 11 kV to 132 kV while the same power flows through the same cables. The heat loss in the cables becomes:
questions.x: The voltage rises 12 times, so the current falls to 1/12. Loss = I²R, so it falls to (1/12)² = 1/144.

questions.q: A capacitor of (250/π) μF is connected to a 50 Hz supply. Its reactance Xc = 1/(2πfC) is:
questions.x: 2πfC = 2π × 50 × 250 × 10⁻⁶/π = 0.025, so Xc = 1/0.025 = 40 Ω. Forgetting to take the reciprocal gives 0.025.

questions.q: To smooth the pulsating output of a rectifier, a component is connected in parallel with the load resistor. This component is a:
questions.x: A capacitor charges during each pulse and discharges through the load between pulses, filling in the gaps and reducing the ripple.

questions.q: Which list puts these photons in order of increasing energy?
o: X-rays, visible light, infrared, radio waves
Infrared, radio waves, X-rays, visible light
Radio waves, infrared, visible light, X-rays
Visible light, infrared, X-rays, radio waves
questions.x: Photon energy increases with frequency. Radio waves have the lowest frequency, then infrared, visible light and X-rays.

questions.q: A continuous spectrum, unlike a line spectrum, contains:
o: All wavelengths over a range, with no gaps
Only dark lines with no bright background
questions.x: A continuous spectrum spreads smoothly over all wavelengths in a range, like that of a hot filament. A line spectrum shows only certain sharp wavelengths.

questions.q: For a small gamma source in air, the dose rate falls with the inverse square of distance. A worker moves from 1 m to 2 m away. Her dose rate becomes:
questions.x: Dose rate ∝ 1/d². Doubling the distance gives 1/2² = 1/4 of the dose rate, which is why distance is a key safety measure.

questions.q: Grandfather was obstinate about his old radio. His children bought him a new one with clear sound and a remote control, but he left it in its box. Every evening he sat with the old set, turning its knob and shaking it when the signal faded, and he refused to hear a word against it. As used in the passage, 'obstinate' means:
questions.x: He keeps the old radio and refuses to listen to any criticism of it, so 'obstinate' means stubborn, unwilling to change his mind. Nothing in the passage shows he is afraid of the new set.

questions.q: Report in indirect speech, a week later: Fatima said, "I must leave now."
o: Fatima said that she has to leave now.
Fatima said that she had to leave then.
Fatima said that she will have to leave then.
Fatima said that I had to leave then.
questions.x: 'Must' expressing necessity can change to 'had to', 'now' becomes 'then', and 'I' becomes 'she'.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly rewrites "If I were in your place, I would apologise" with inversion?
o: I were in your place, I would apologise.
Was I in your place, I would apologise.
Were I in your place, I would apologise.
If were I in your place, I would apologise.
questions.x: In a conditional, 'if' can be dropped by putting 'were' before the subject: 'Were I ...'.

questions.q: Which sentence uses verbal irony?
o: The weather was perfect, so the class went on a picnic.
Heavy rain flooded the classroom, so the picnic was cancelled.
Looking at the flooded classroom, the teacher said, "What perfect weather for a picnic."
The teacher said the picnic would be held when the rain stopped.
questions.x: Verbal irony means saying the opposite of what is meant; calling a flood 'perfect weather for a picnic' is clearly not meant literally.

questions.q: "The medicine alleviated Hamza's headache within minutes, and he was soon able to sleep peacefully." The word 'alleviated' means:
questions.x: To 'alleviate' is to make pain or trouble less severe; he could sleep afterwards, so the pain was eased, not worsened.

questions.q: Report in indirect speech: Hamza said to his friends, "Let us go for a walk."
o: Hamza told his friends that let us go for a walk.
Hamza ordered his friends that they go for a walk.
Hamza suggested to his friends that they should go for a walk.
Hamza asked his friends to let us go for a walk.
questions.x: 'Let us' as a proposal is reported with 'suggested ... that they should ...'.

questions.q: A rider is being reminded about safety. In which version is the frequency adverb 'always' placed correctly after 'must'?
o: You must wear always a helmet on a motorbike.
You must wear a helmet on always a motorbike.
You must always wear a helmet on a motorbike.
You must a helmet always wear on a motorbike.
questions.x: With a modal or auxiliary, an adverb of frequency goes after the modal and before the main verb.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: "Neither Ali nor I ____ ready for the test."
questions.x: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. The nearer subject is 'I', so the verb is 'am'.

questions.q: Which question tag correctly completes the sentence? "Let's go for a walk after dinner, ____?"
questions.x: A suggestion beginning with 'Let's' (let us) takes the tag 'shall we?'. 'Isn't it' is a common error and does not match any verb in the sentence.

questions.q: Which reason gives a sound basis for believing that a news report is true?
o: It has been shared by many people on social media
It is written in an exciting and dramatic style
It is confirmed by several independent and reliable sources
It agrees with what the reader already believed
questions.x: Independent, reliable confirmation is evidence. Popularity, style and agreement with our own views do not show that a report is true.

questions.q: Argument: "Our town's air is cleaner this year because the brick kilns switched to cleaner technology." Which fact, if true, most strengthens this argument?
o: The town had much more rain than usual this year
The new kiln technology was expensive to install
Nearby towns whose kilns did not switch showed no improvement in their air
Many people in the town bought new cars this year
questions.x: If similar towns without the change did not improve, the kilns become the likely reason. Extra rain would offer another explanation and so weaken the argument.

questions.q: Find the next number: 5, 15, 45, 135, ?
questions.x: Each term is 3 times the one before: 135 x 3 = 405.

questions.q: Find the next letter: E, I, M, Q, ?
questions.x: Each letter moves 4 places forward: E(5), I(9), M(13), Q(17), so next is U(21).

questions.q: Given that no P is Q and every R is Q, which statement must be true?
questions.x: Every R lies inside Q, and no P lies inside Q, so no R can be P. Nothing says every Q is an R, and the statements about some P being R contradict the conclusion.

questions.q: P, Q, R, S and W are five boxes of different weights. P is heavier than Q. Q is heavier than S. R is lighter than S. If W is lighter than R, which box is in the middle by weight?
questions.x: From heaviest: P, Q, S, R, W. The third of five is S.

questions.q: Statement: Workers in a factory complain of hearing problems, and noise in the main hall is measured far above the safe limit. Courses of action: I. Workers should be given ear protection, and the noise reduced where possible. II. Workers' hearing should be tested at regular intervals. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: Action I reduces the harm at its source, and action II detects damage early. Both are practical steps based on the measured problem.

questions.q: In a garden, plants placed in the shade of a high wall grew poorly, while the same kind of plants in the open, given the same soil and water, grew well. What is the most likely cause?
o: The wall made the soil more fertile
The open plants were given more water
Plants cannot grow near any wall
The plants in the wall's shade received less sunlight
questions.x: Soil and water were the same, so the difference lies in light. Plants need sunlight to make food, and the wall's shade reduced it.

questions.q: A man says, "Vaccines make children ill, because my nephew had a mild fever the day after his vaccination." Which is a valid argument against his claim?
o: A short mild fever can be a normal reaction, and one case cannot outweigh large studies showing vaccines prevent disease
His nephew is too young to have a fever
Doctors never give more than one vaccine
questions.x: A brief mild fever is a known, usually harmless reaction to some vaccines. One case cannot overturn evidence from large studies that vaccines protect against disease.
